inlineContent.text: WorldModule is built around a
, a value that holds everything your game or simulation
knows. The world organizes that state with a few simple ideas:
An
entity
is one thing in the world, such as a ball, a player or a particle. It has no data
of its own; you refer to it by its handle, an
A
component
is a plain value that an entity holds, such as a position or a health total.
Any type that conforms to
can be a component, and an entity holds at most one
component of each type.
A
resource
is a value the world holds once, outside any entity, such as a clock or a score.
Any type that conforms to
can be a resource.
The examples throughout this module’s documentation use these components:

code: struct Position: Component { var x: Double, y: Double }
struct Velocity: Component { var dx: Double, dy: Double }
struct Health: Component { var current: Int }
struct Name: Component, Hashable { var value: String }

content.text: Spawn Entities and Work with Their Components

inlineContent.text: Spawn an entity with the components it starts with. The world returns the entity’s handle, which
you use to read and change its components:

code: let hero = world.spawn(Name(value: "Ada"), Position(x: 0, y: 0), Health(current: 100))

Most of the work in a game applies to every entity that holds some set of components: every
entity with a position and a velocity moves, every entity with health can take damage. A query
visits those entities and reads their components, and an update changes one component of each in
place:

code: struct Elapsed: Resource { var seconds: Double }

storage until one of them changes, so copying is cheap, and keeping an earlier state for undo, a
replay or a comparison takes one assignment. To keep a world beyond the life of your program,
